To the Editor of The Tribune—,

Sir: Recent issues of your esteemed Journal onto no desire to explain the causes which have led to the present remarkable and peculiar condition existing in the local Office of the steamboat inspection service, and if a service there is.

Years will enable me to assist you in so doing.

Permit me, then, to suggest that the steamboat inspection service exists for the purpose, primarily, of inspecting steam vessels in order that the lives and property of those using them may be guarded. It would be in order, then, to ascertain whether inspections are made of steam vessels in this port. You will be astonished, and if you also if you give publicity to this letter, if not for if any inspections of steam vessels are made in this harbor although they all possess certificates saying that they have been inspected, and are safe and seaworthy for the business which they engage. To ascertain this should be the first step toward REFORM.

When the owner or the agent of a steamer, on inspection, the steamer's name and where he is located are entered in a book, and also an assistant inspector of hulls and an assistant inspector of boilers are assigned; a blank form is filled out which directs each assistant to go for inspection the said steamer. The reverse of this blank form requires the assistant inspector to make the statement that the said steamer was inspected at such and such hours. But the assistants sent to examine hulls and returning say that the steamer was inspected, but are not required to say that they inspected it.

The problem now arises: Who did inspect the vessel? The law requires that the vessels be inspected, and the law also requires that the local inspectors, not the assistants, shall inspect them. In a matter of fact, the assistants are supposed to inspect. If you are permitted to examine any letters they write supplementary to their examinations, you will find over and over again, that they use the word inspect as defining what they have done instead of examine, which they are directed to do. This is a technical point. The local inspectors do not accompany the assistants on these examinations; sometimes the assistants may be at Perth Amboy, or at Northport, or at Sing Sing or Peekskill, or at all these points the same day, and it would be impossible for the local inspectors to be present personally at all of these places at the same hour on the same day.

In 1870 a solicitor of the Treasury Department stated that in the exercise of duties involving discretion and judgment those duties could not be delegated, and the decision further stated that assistant inspectors are not empowered to perform any of the duties devolving upon local inspectors. So the law requiring local inspectors to inspect and the law officer of the Treasury Department having declared that they may not delegate any duty to assistants, and that assistant inspectors may not perform any of the duties of local inspectors, and it being physically impossible for the local inspectors to inspect all of the steam vessels in their district, expedients are resorted to which necessitate a violation of the law instead of rectification. Were the officers of the steamboat inspection service to make it clear that the duties imposed upon local inspectors in the port of New-York cannot be complied with, and that the law is therefore evaded in order to get the semblance of an inspection of steam vessels, I believe that Congress would immediately rectify such an anomaly. And I assert that the executive officers of this bureau are conniving at fraud rather than to request the change that is so sadly needed.

If steam vessels thus alleged to have been inspected meet with disaster traceable to the incompetency or neglect of the assistant inspectors who examined them for inspection, and asserted that they had been inspected, the local inspectors who make affidavits that they inspected the steamer, that they found her safe and seaworthy, that they found her possessed of the equipment set forth upon the face of said certificate, when as a matter of fact, the local inspectors who swear had never personally examined the vessel or her equipment—the local inspectors, say, liable to ten years in the penitentiary, the accident involves loss of life and of official negligence. This is very serious. In affairs local inspectors making affidavits to facts which they know nothing personally about, is excepted through the reports of assistants. In a case where a boat was burned at Hell Gate, the jury stood six to six, but if they had agreed that the inspectors would have been liable to ten years imprisonment. And yet the boat was inspected by Andrew Craft and it was asserted that these men were incompetent; their conduct was never investigated. They continued for years afterward to examine vessels for inspection which one might say they ever in to swear that they did.

The local inspectors never have any voice in the selection and appointment of these assistants whose acts at any time may land the locals in the penitentiary.

In 1885 an assistant inspector by the name of Patrick Reilly was appointed whom local inspectors were desirous of retaining their positions. Twice Local Inspector Mathews made the man refuse to perform the duty for which he was appointed. Mathews was summarily removed for alleged insubordination. Assistants since this incident, local inspectors for paltry salary of $2,200 a year, are willing to constantly stand in the SHADOW of the penitentiary, liable to become an inmate at any time because of the dereliction of any one of their sixteen assistants, and it is equally remarkable that they are permitted to go scot-free, no matter how terrible the consequence of their incompetency or these alleged examinations for inspection or inspections.

What value can attach to a service where the men who assume the responsibility are penalizable and yet make no effort to have the law changed? If what we say here to state that so much of the safety from disaster on steam vessels we may well believe does not result from such methods or perversions, is true, then we must say that if any injury results, it is due to the inefficiency of the service.

I am here to state that so able a jurist as the Attorney General attached his name to a statement which declared that the duties of assistant inspectors are not the same as those of local inspectors. Yet this statement is twelve years old, despite which the same conditions exist. What must one think of the efficiency of the service so administered to leave uncorrected such glaring anomalies? Therefore, as a result of twelve years in that service and of fifteen years close observation of the service, I have publicly stated these abuses, but they still remain uncorrected.

To verify what I have alleged, ask you to assign a representative of your journal to visit the local inspectors' office in this port, and to ask to be shown the blanks used in assigning assistant inspectors for duty, and that you carefully note the wording of the blank, and the writing filed in by the assistants, and that you also examine the certificates of inspection issued, how they are filled out and by whom their facts sworn to. Ask if a small rubber stamp is not used to indicate in an obscure corner of these certificates that they were "Inspected by -- assistant inspector of hulls."

burg.


The June term of the Hastings Court
of Petersburg, Judge J. N. Mullen,
presiding, opened this morning at 11
o'clock. The grand jury found two
presentments for felony. There were
no cases of special interest disposed of
on the criminal docket.


William Allen, colored, witness in
the case of Thomas King, charged with
felony, was fined $40 for not being in
court to answer to his name when it
was called. He was committed to jail
in default of payment of the fine.

Mullen fixed July 9th for hearing
arguments upon the confirmation of
the commissioner's report in the cases
of the Farmers Loan and Trust Com-
pany vs. the Petersburg Street Railway
Company, the McGuire manufactur-
ing Company vs. the same, and the
Farmers Loan and Trust Company vs.
the Petersburg and Asylum Railway
Company. Important questions con-
cerning the priorities of the various
debts of the two companies, especially
the street railway company, are in
volved, and there is a large array of
counsel representing the conflicting
interests.

Catholic School took place this morn-
ing and were quite largely attended.

itation, to Miss Lizzie Collins; oil

ries, it is an attractive decoration for

leaves curl and crackle in the heat and
flame.


The evergreen tree is symbol used
as the revival of nature, which, astro-
-nomically, signifies the return of the
sun. Hung with lights and offerings,

the principal characteristics of Christ.
mastide.-New York Mercury,

News and Observer.


There seems to be some division of sentiment among the republican bosses on the silver question. A few days ago we copied an interview with Congressman Settle in which he put himself on record strongly against free coinage.


A few days after Settle's interview, his chief rival as the boss of the republican party, Senator Pritchard, said:


"I am for the free and unlimited coinage of silver. The great majority of the North Carolina republicans are for it. In fact, all are friendly to silver."


This seemed to make the issue plain between them. The Winston Republican comes to Settle's help and says:


"About nine-tenths of the republicans are opposed to free and unlimited coinage and do not propose to be dumped, bag and baggage into the laps of our populist friends."


And now comes A. Z. Holton, chairman of the State Republican Executive committee, in a letter to Rich. Mond Pearson, taking the grounds for fusion on State offices, but against it in the National fight. We quote:


"Under the resolutions (which Butler had passed in the Silver Convention) neither Reid, McKinley nor Allison could hope to get their supporters for even five electors and it would be folly for us to talk about voting for populist electors, and it would be folly for us to talk about voting for populist electors when they declare they will not support our part of the ticket for no one expects the National republican platform to declare for the free and unlimited coinage of silver, independent of international agreement, or to nominate a free silver candidate for the presidency."


We cannot afford to condemn the policy of the national republican party solely to effect fusion, nor can a republican advocate the populist doctrine and hope to retain the confidence of his party.


He will either have to abandon his position or fall in line with the populists. The sooner our people realize this the better for themselves and the party.


There is cold comfort to Pritchard in all this.

found in the retirement and cancellation of
greenbacks, and the outstanding treasury

count.

by renewed activity and enterprise in all
business circles, the restored confidence at

readers will be able to follow the case and not
waste time on the reading of immaterial mat
ter. This is to be commended, and we predict
that THE CALL will lie in extraordinary de-
mand, especially while the case continues.
Its one-minute synopsis is a gem.-Vallejo
Chronicle.


THE CALL declares its intention to report the
Durrant trial without pruriency. That is the
sort of thing that good people have long been
wanting to see in San Francisco journalism,
and now there is a chance to determine
whether they are in earnest about it, and
whether there is enough of them to pay.-Ala-
media Argus.


The San Francisco CALL seems really to have
enlisted for the war in its fight against un-
cleanness. Its latest promise is to this effect,
that it will waste no space in reporting the
Durrant trial, that the reader will be given a
comprehensive understanding of the case with
out his wading through useless columns of un-
interesting and tiresome details, that all objec-
tionable features will be eliminated to the
greatest possible degree. That's right. Thus
far in newspaper dealings with this case, there
has beeen more of desire to crafty morbid
and prurient tastes and gather the nickels this
exercise would ensure, than to meet the re-
quirements OF normal minds.-Napa Register.

TO our agricultural prosperity. By a systematic saving of much of the material, which is often wasted by even intelligent farmers, we can at nominal expense return to the soil much of that which is taken from it in the different gathered crops. All vegetable and animal accumulation round the barns and stables, the fowl houses, fence corners, the woodpile, even the ashes and slops from the houses, and the leaves, which so often accumulate in unsightly heaps around our dwellings, may be considered so much ready material from which we form compounds of equal value with any commercial fertilizer that we buy at such heavy expense. In the present condition of our agriculture we cannot discard commercial fertilizers. We must still rely on these, and, judiciously used, they contribute largely to our success.

Our mistake has been that we have depended too entirely on these, and consigned to useless inactivity the rich stores of plant food that accumulate on every farm. These should constitute the principal factor in any plan of fertilization, with the commercial goods as an adjunct, rather than the reverse. In making a compost heap, a good plan where leaves are abundant and close at hand is to put a layer of leaves about 2 inches deep, then a layer of manure, about six inches deep, then a layer of scrapings of rich earth six inches deep. If ashes or lime can be had they will aid materially in the decomposition of the heap. Put on the different layers, packing down firmly, until the heap is six or eight feet high, keeping the sides well squared up and the middle a little lower. If there should not be sufficient rain, dampen the heap by pouring on water. In the spring, just before time to haul out to the fields, tear down the heap and mix thoroughly. The real cost of such a heap, say about 4 feet square, would be equal to about a ton of guano, but intrinsically it would be worth at least twice as much.

The fields which are covered with mass of vegetable growth should be turned under as soon as possible in order to give the mass more time to decompose. Do not turn under too deeply, the decay will take place more rapidly near the surface. There are on an average many more bright working days in December than in January or February, which is another reason why the work should not be delayed. If the plowing is to be done in a cornfield, when the fodder and corn have been pulled and the bare stalks left standing there is often much difficulty in completely covering the stalks. They remain partly on the surface, and becoming only imperfectly decayed, the benefit of any plant food they may contain is lost to the succeeding crop. Their presence is also a hindrance to thorough and neat work. As long as we continue the present plan of gathering corn, and stripping the fodder from the stalks this difficulty will be encountered and until we settle on some more economical plan of saving the stalk entire we must consider the best methods of getting these stalks in condition, not only to benefit but to interfere as little as possible with the cultivation of the crop which follows. A good plan, which has been successfully tried is to select a frosty morning and run a heavy two-horse roller over the field. The stalks being brittle, break more easily, and the roller in passing over them not only forces them into the ground, but the heavy pressure fattens and breaks them apart in such way as to give freer entrance to moisture and frost two powerful agents in breaking down their structure.

(special.)—The Goodman trial was resumed and the prisoner came into court early this morning.

We had been held in reserve on the second day at Gettysburg so long that men and horses became nervous and afraid. My horse was an old veteran who would drop his head and pick at the grass with battery firing on either side of us, but as the moments dragged away on this occasion he evinced woman's nervousness. A tremor of excitement—a sort of shiver—ran down the line.


The wind had shifted bit to blew the smoke to our left, and down across the meadows we saw the Confederate cavalry forming, with the green woods for background. Jeb Stuart's men were there, Ashby's men, men from Hampton's legion, Imboden's Virginians, Rosser's rangers, guerrillas from Mosby command. There were fragments from every cavalry command we had met in the turnpikes of old Virginia, and there wasn't a squadron which wouldn't stand for a charge. The battery began firing more rapidly, and there was not a man of us who did not realize what was coming long enough before we got the word. Some of the horses knew it too. You could feel them filling their lungs and stringing up their nerves for hard work.


"They are going to charge our battery!" was the exclamation on every man's lips, but we could not be sure of just the part we were to play in the affair. If dismounted and used as infantry to support the guns, we could make desperate fight of it, and for several minutes we listened to hear such an order given. During this time an aid rode up with an order to the colonel. It was an order from the general to retire the battery. It had come too late. Some of the battery horses had been killed and number of others wounded by the explosions of the big shells thrown at us from the woods behind the Confederate cavalry, and the way to the rear was all blocked by the ammunition wagons which had come up. The battery would be lost or saved right where it stood.


At the end of five minutes while we yet sat waiting the troopers in gray wheeled into line under a fire which must have tried the nerves of the bravest, and then the compact mass got the word to advance. They were coming for our battery, which was without infantry supports. There stood two thin, short lines, representing a thousand dragoons, but not numbering one-half of that figure and body of men.

at his watch, each time thinking that
surely the hour had arrived, and when at
length it came he set forth with sinking
dread lest something had happened to de-
lay Martin, lest they should exasperate
Elsie's captors to murder.


Martin had told him not to search the
mine. He therefore hurried through it as
fast as he could in the darkness, and
stepped instantaneously into the ice-cold
water of the shaft. It may have been that
the shock of the water reacted upon his
nerves; at all events, his head seemed
clearer, his confidence greater, as he walked
along and though his heart beat high
when he dragged himself up into the drier
tunnel of the cave, he felt that his fingers
would be steady on the trigger if there
should he need to shoot.


He had been at pains to make no splash-
ing noise as he waded through the shaft,
and now he walked with the utmost eau-
tion. Slowly, very slowly he proceeded,
feeling with one hand along one side of
the cavern, and testing each step before
he bore his weight down. He paused just
an instant at frequent intervals to listen.


Suddenly he heard something, what he
could not tell. He stopped and listened.
It came again, stealthy, fearful.
"Jack!" whispered Will, crouching down.
"Billy," came the whispered response,
and at the same instant a sound that filled
both men with horror.


It was an inarticulate, gurgling scream,
a woman's voice, and it seemed to come
from directly in front of Will.


Martin had told him to lie flat down, and
he was obeying the injunction, and just
as the scream rang all but in his ears, his
outstretched hand came in contact with a
human body.

To the Editor of the Inter-State.

SIR:—I have read with interest the
Interview between Mr. A. W. Campbell,
of your paper, and Mr. B. T. Nelson, of
St. Louis, supreme reporter of the
Knights of Honor, concerning the com-
parative merits of fraternal protection
and "life" life insurance. With
much that Mr. Nelson says I heartily
agree. He is right, for instance, in his
claim that the sole excuse for the ex-
istence of such organizations is that
protection may be furnished to one's
dependents in the event of premature
death, and that they cannot be made
available as a means of investment for
investment's sake. No life insurance
organization can offer anything worthy
the name of investment in connection
with a life insurance contract, though it
is quite true that agents sometimes rep-
resent it to the public in this form. It
is only an investment in that it necessi-
tates savings on the part of many per-
sons of the sums paid for premiums on
the policies, which, otherwise, would be
wasted in extravagances.

I am compelled to admit the force of
rigid economy exercised in the manage-
ment of the affairs of the Knights of
Honor. This is worthy of all praise and
might properly be emulated by the
great life insurance companies, whose
wastefulness in some instances is notorious.

However, concerning the plan of the
K. of H., which Mr. Nelson defends
with such zeal and seeming plausibili-
ty, I am wholly at variance with him.
In saying this I do not wish to detract
a particle from the credit his order does
serve for the good it has done within
the past twenty years. Indeed, as he
says, an organization which has been
the means of distributing among widows
and orphans the enormous sum of
nearly fifty millions of dollars is deserv-
ing of all praise and I fully accord
mine. My regret is that the faulty
plan upon which it is founded gives lit-
tle ground for hope that its good work
can long be continued. I do not share
Mr. Nelson's view that the organization
can be perpetuated by good manage-
ment, if by that he means merely hon-
est management without radical re-
casting of its methods.

Mr. Nelson is disposed to attribute
the steady increase in the order's death
rate in the past to carelessness in the
selection of its earlier membership.
I am inclined to the simpler explanation
that old men die at greater rate per
thousand than do young ones. This
fact has in great part been lost sight
of in the formulation of the scheme of as-
sessments of the Knights of Honor. It
is true, according to the present pub-
lished table of rates, that on admission
members are charged at different rates,
beginning with so cents, for age thirty
and under, and increasing to 50 for age
fifty. It may be remarked in passing
that these rates, in their relation to each
other, do not represent the true ratio of
hazard as expressed in the accepted
tables of mortality, but this is not a vital
matter. It is a vital error, however,
that the initial rate should be retained
throughout one's membership in the
order—for through it we have the
anomaly of two members varying wide-
ly in age securing the same amount of
protection at identically the same cost,
or, to put it another way, two mem-
bers of the same age and having the same
protection at widely varying cost.

To illustrate: Let us assume Mr. Nel-
son entered the order twenty-one years
ago at the age of twenty-nine, paying a
assessment rate of eighty cents, and
which rate he continues to pay now. It
then appears that he, man of fifty, is
paying for his protection precisely the
same, and no more, than his newly ad-
mitted brother, aged thirty or less. Now
no one disputes the fact that deaths are
more frequent per 1000 among men of
fifty than among those aged under thirty.

Equity requires, that each member
contribute in proportion to the burden
he imposes on the order, but this is not
done, for it is evident that Mr. Nelson
and the earlier membership are paying
less than their fair share of the death
costs, and naturally it follows that the
new recruits are called upon to make
good the shortage. This makes clear
why Mr. Nelson is compelled to admit
that a young man of twenty-one pays
to the Knights of Honor just
about what he would be called
upon to pay for an ordinary life
policy in a life insurance company,
and about twice the actual value of the
protection he enjoys. He admits further
that a policy in life insurance com-
pany would have some value for sur-
render after two or three years, but un-
dertakes to offset this by the advantage
the membership of the Knights of
Honor enjoys in being able to pay in
installments. He forgets that most life
insurance companies offer similar priv-
ileges.

As a matter of fact young men of thir-
ty and under can secure the same pro-
tection in other fraternal orders, in as-

at about one-half the actual annual out-
lay required in the Knights of Honor;
or if they choose to pay the Knights of
Honor cost, the regular companies will
accumulate a considerable share of it
which may be withdrawn in after years
when the need of protection ceases.

companies of the better class are in
every way more desirable for young
men in that, for about the same cost,
certainly as complete protection is fur-
nished and in addition cash value for
the insured himself in case of need.

To the Mayor and Board Of Aldermen,
men of the city Of Manitowoc,

The Manitowoc Terminal Company respectfully represents:

The completion of the 10 and 12 foot channel so-called, between Buffalo and Chicago and Duluth will work a tremendous change in the character of commerce in Lake Michigan. Vessels drawing twenty feet instead of fourteen feet will then require accommodation at docks and wharves, and harbor facilities must be provided for them.

Few people appreciate how soon this change in the very basis of lake commerce will be actually accomplished. Next year will see it in operation and no time is to be lost in preparing the harbor of Manitowoc for these great vessels.

The United States engineers officially state that the contracts require completion of all the eight sections of the channel by the close of the season of 1895; that three of these sections are already finished; that fair progress is being made on the rest and that there is good chance for completion of them all within the contract time, excepting that section eight mouth of Detroit river possibly may not be entirely done this autumn.

Vessels of heavy burden and deep draught have always proved most economical. It is quite plain therefore that water freights between Lake Erie ports and Lake Michigan ports will very soon go in vessels and steamers drawing twenty feet. Those harbors on Lake Michigan which are not ready next year to accommodate such steamers and vessels will be at great disadvantage. Manitowoc harbor, having unexcelled natural facilities and open water during the entire year, ought at once to be made capable of receiving them. At present, no harbors on Lake Michigan can do this, and slight preparation has yet been made anywhere for this radical change in the character of shipping between Lake Erie ports and those on Lake Michigan.

The Manitowoc Terminal Company, being deeply impressed with the wisdom of making Manitowoc harbor ready without delay for the accommodation of vessels drawing twenty feet, and of improving all the bridges and harbor approaches to suit these large vessels, now urge upon your Honorable body the importance of appointing a SPECIAL STANDING COMMITTEE to act for the city of Manitowoc which shall have power, without delay and in all efficient ways, to cooperate with the Manitowoc Terminal Company in preparing docks and slips and harbor facilities for the accommodation of steamers and all other vessels drawing twenty feet. It respectfully submits that the importance to the City Of Manitowoc of being able to accommodate such large vessels as soon as they enter Lake Michigan, can hardly be overestimated. It asks that this committee may be empowered to confer with the different business interests which will be affected, and that it be authorized also to negotiate for the construction of bridges and other public works and report to you its recommendations, in order that all plans may be harmonized for rendering Manitowoc one of the very best possible harbors for accommodation of big vessels on Lake Michigan. It also represents the importance of taking immediate steps to induce the United States further to develop, improve and profess the harbor of Manitowoc and its approaches, and it urges that the Special Committee on the Harbor be empowered to do everything which is expedient or necessary to lay facts before the Congress of the United States. It further urges upon your Honorable body that the municipal authorities forthwith take such action as the charter of the city permits for dredging or aiding to dredge the channel of Manitowoc River to depth sufficient to accommodate vessels drawing twenty feet, and secure cooperation, so far as it is possible, between the municipal authorities and the owners of lots bounding on said river in procuring this uniform depth throughout the channel. Your petitioner is now the owner of large amount of property fronting on said river and is getting ready to dredge along its own water frontage for the accommodation of vessels of twenty feet draft. The appointment of Special Committee on the Harbor to represent the city authorities of Manitowoc will greatly aid the completion of this public improvement, which your petitioner believes to be the most important for the prosperity of the city which has ever been undertaken since it was founded.

Dated Manitowoc May 9th, 1895.

MANITOWOC TERMINAL COMPANY.
Sgd EDGAR C. Hoe, Secretary.

Attest.
Sgd Z. B. GREENLEAF, President.

Washington, Aug. 9.—Acting Secretary Adee has received advices from United States Consul General Jermigan at Shanghai, dated July 8, inclosing four letters received by him from missionaries giving in great detail accounts of the trouble in China leading up to the riots against the missionaries at Cheng Tu in the province of Szechuen.

One of these from Spencer Lanier, very comprehensive in scope, dated Chun keng, China, says that West China mission of the Methodist Episcopal church is the only American mission represented at Cheng Tu. This mission owned one piece of property in Cheng Tu in which was Chinese building for the residence of the two families, a Chinese building used as chapel, a dispensary and minor structures. Mr. Lanier says that substantially all these are gone, even the paving stones being carried out of the courts. The total loss exclusive of personal losses is about 6000 taels. The American Baptist Missionary Union had stations at Sui Fu, Kiating and Yacho. The mission and personal property at Kiating and Yacho is probably all lost though particulars had not been received by Mr. Lanier when his letter was written. At Sui Fu the Americans owned a great deal of property, but not much damage was done to it.

In the attack on the premises of the Canadian Methodist mission, the two physicians in charge of the hospital and chapel, which were afterwards looted and burned, applied to the officials for assistance, but they would give none, although several of them were quite near. Late that evening, May 28, the members of the American Methodist mission sought refuge in the district magistrate's Yamen, but were refused, and told they would be protected if they returned home.

Relying on this promise, they were unprepared for the mob which soon visited them, and had barely time to escape. Operations were renewed by the mob at daybreak next day and before noon the attack was general on all Catholic and Protestant mission places. The American Methodists from their hillside only few feet away watched the mob for twelve hours plundering their homes. Some of the 20,000 soldiers of the province assisted in the looting and dug up a number of bones which they took to the district magistrate's Yamen representing them to be the bones of babies which the foreigners had eaten. and the preservation of national honor and credit, am not willing to see gold entirely banished from our currency and finances.

In my opinion the secretary of the treasury should be authorized to issue bonds of the government for the purpose of procuring and maintaining sufficient gold reserve and the redemption and cancellation of the United States legal tender notes and the treasury notes issued for the purchase of silver under the law of July 14, 1893. We should be relieved from the humiliating process of issuing bonds to procure gold to be immediately and repeatedly drawn out on these obligations for purposes not related to the benefit of our government or our people. The principal and interest of these bonds should be payable on their face in gold, because they should be sold only for gold or its representative and because there would now probably be difficulty in favorably disposing of bonds not containing this stipulation.

I suggest that the bonds be issued in denominations of $20 and $50 and their multiples, and that they bear interest at a rate not exceeding per cent. per annum. I do not see why they should not be payable fifty years from their dates. We of the present generation have large amounts to pay if we meet our obligations, and long bonds are most salable. The secretary of the treasury might well be permitted at his discretion to receive on the sale of bonds the legal tender and treasury notes to be retired, and of course when they are thus retired or redeemed in gold they should be cancelled.

These bonds under existing laws could be deposited in national banks as security for circulation up to the face value of these or any other bonds so deposited except bonds outstanding bearing only per cent interest and which sell in the market at less than par.

National banks should not be allowed to take out circulating notes of less denomination than $10 and when such as are now outstanding reach the treasurer, except for redemption and retirement, they should be cancelled, and notes of the denomination of $10 and upwards issued in their stead. Silver certificates of the denomination of $10 and upwards should be replaced by certificates of denomination under $10.

Objection has been made to the issuance of interest bearing obligations for the purpose of retiring the non-interest bearing legal tender notes. In point of fact, however, these notes have burdened us with a large amount of interest and it is still accumulating. The aggregate interest on the original issue of bonds, the proceeds of which in gold bonds constitute the reserve for the payment of the notes, amounted to $70,326,250 on January 1, 1895, and the annual charge for interest on these bonds and those issued for the same purpose during the last year will be $9,145,000, dating from January 1, 1895.

While the cancellation of these notes would not relieve us from the obligations incurred on their account, these figures are given by way of suggesting that their existence has not been free from interest charges, and that the longer they are outstanding, judging from the experience of the last year, the more expensive will they become.

In conclusion I desire to frankly confess my reluctance to issuing more bonds in present circumstances and with no better results than have lately followed that course. I am adding an assurance of my anxiety to cooperate with the present congress in any reasonable measure of relief an expression of my determination to leave nothing undone which furnishes hope for improving the situation or checking suspicion of our disinclination or disability to meet with the strictest honor every national obligation.

nest! When the plundered bird returned

was repeated as soon as she was again

repeated many times, with the result

grew apace! In the same place a nest
remained undisturbed, and was occu-
pied by probably the same pair of birds
for several seasons. One spring they re-
turned and all appeared prosperous, I'M
til one day it was noticed that a num-

ing up the entrance to this old nest.

new nest over the old, was soon COM
pleted. The closed nest was then brok-
en- open and within was found the dead

ably died a natural death, and the

Dr. Knowlton's observations are as follows: Within my collecting grounds is a shed open only on one side, where for many years cliff swallows have attached their nests to the sleepers of the loft. In the spring of 1873 they returned, as usual, and soon began repairing old nests or building new ones. One day it was noticed that one bird remained in her half-finished nest, and did not appear to be much engaged. Soon neighbour, owning a nest a few feet away, arrived with fresh pellet of clay, and after adjusting it in a satisfactory manner flew away for more. No sooner was she out of sight than the quiet bird repaired to the neighbour's nest, appropriated the fresh clay and nodded it to her own nest! When the plundered bird returned no notice was taken of the theft, which was repeated as soon as she was again out of sight. These movements were repeated many times, with the result that the nest of the stay-at-home bird grew apace! In the same place a nest remained undisturbed, and was occupied by probably the same pair of birds for several seasons. One spring they returned and all appeared prosperous, until one day it was noticed that a number of swallows were engaged in walling up the entrance to this old nest. This work, as well as the outline of a new nest over the old, was soon completed. The closed nest was then broken open and within was found the dead body of a swallow. The bird had probably died a natural death, and the friends, being unable to remove the body and knowing that it would soon become offensive, adopted this method of sealing it up.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 15.—The Spanish minister, Senor Dupuy de Lome, has called the attention of the State Department to the rumor that the American steamer Laurada has violated the neutrality laws of the United States in landing arms on Cuban soil to aid the insurgents there. Secretary Olney has transmitted Senor de Lome's protest to the Treasury Department and Secretary Carlisle to-day telegraphed collector of customs to look out for the Laurada and to seize her wherever found. The Department of Justice had also been advised of Minister de Lome's communication and United States marshals have been instructed to cooperate with the Treasury officials in detaining the vessel when found.

The Laurada was formerly the British steamer Express and was given an American registry by a special bill passed through the last Congress. She is supposed to have cleared New York about the 21st of October for Jamaica ports. It is alleged that after leaving port she took on board at some point on Long Island Sound, Emanuel Cespedes, a Cuban leader and his followers, together with large lot of arms and ammunitions. The arms and ammunitions are said to have been landed near Barracoa on the island of Cuba during the night time, and from that point the vessel proceeded to Jamaica. She has since returned to New York, where she left, after being in port few hours, and it is now alleged that she is anchored 16 miles off the coast of Delaware for the purpose of escaping the penalties imposed for violation of the neutrality laws of the United States. Captain Hughes, her commander, is said to have left his ship and his whereabouts is unknown.

Secretary Carlisle is very much impressed with the evidence that has been submitted to him by the Spanish minister regarding the Laurada and is using every means in his power to find the alleged filibustering vessel. While it cannot be asserted positively, it is understood that he has instructed Captain Shoemaker, chief of the revenue marine service, Treasury Department, to dispatch revenue cutters in search of her. The nearest cutter to where the Laurada is supposed to be anchored, is the Alexander Hamilton, stationed at Philadelphia.

If reports be true that the Laurada is 16 miles off the coast of Delaware, the interesting question is presented, it is said, for the first time of attempting to seize an American vessel on the high seas for violation of American laws committed within the marine jurisdiction of the United States. Secretary Carlisle is said to have no doubt of the power of the United States to make such seizure. Should the vessel be found the question of the legality of such seizure, together with the further question as to whether she was really engaged in a filibustering expedition against Cuba in violation of the neutrality laws of the United States, will have to be decided by the courts in this country before the vessel is held and her owners and captain punished.

Revival Services To Commence at First


III. II. Church Tomorrow Night.


Yesterday morning, at the First Methodist Episcopal church, the Rev. W. A. Shanklin preached on The Importance of Evangelistic Work, a sermon preparatory to the special revival services to be held tomorrow evening under the auspices of Rev. G. H. Yaiman, of New York. The preacher emphasized the fact that a revival is the joint work of God and man, rectifying the idea among members of the church that they can do nothing, that the work is not all dependent on them. Every person has an influence, and each generally has more direct influence on certain individuals than all other persons together. That influence may be used to bring them to Christ, or to keep them from Him. Whatever may oppose this view of the subject explains why revivals are often so limited—but few members of the church engage in them. The majority are mere honorary members, doing no work.


The Rev. G. H. Yaiman, of New York city, who comes to lead in the special services, beginning tomorrow, Tuesday, evening, is one of the most eminent Christian workers now living. In New York, Brooklyn, Philadelphia and the other great cities of the East multitudes have crowded to his services and thousands have been converted. Mr. Yaiman was at Ocean Grove for twelve years, and from his leadership thereof his fame has gone to all quarters of the globe, although his work has, until within the last two years, been altogether in the East. G. H. Yaiman. Great success has attended this movement. This, in this city, where there are such crowds of non-churchgoing people, is remarkable and hopeful."

Neither Mr. Belmont nor Mr. Morgan is willing to make public the transaction of the syndicate which they head, so a great deal of curiosity about the sale of the new bonds is likely to go unqualified. After all it is only necessary that the public know that the contract is faithfully carried out. There are no indications that it will not be. It was charged in Congress the other day that the syndicate could not control the sterling exchange market, and that if it could it would not do so any longer than it took to market the bonds and so on. It is needless to point out how illogical such arguments are. So far the market has been managed. Last week exchange rose to figure that would have made gold exports profitable, but the big exporting firms made no attempt to ship any of the precious metal. They knew that if they did go by the time the gold reached Europe the market would be down and the shipments would be at loss. The syndicate sold enough sterling bills to bring down prices, as there was not even a fury. As we have stated before, the syndicate can control the sterling market; they have been in that business, at least the Rothschilds have, for centuries. It is said by good authorities that credit of $500,000,000 in Europe properly drawn against would have been sufficient to stop the gold movement at any time between 1884 and 1890. In fact, these gold exports were checked entirely in the spring of 1888 by drawing against some heavy lots of railway securities that had been placed abroad.

That part of the contract which binds the syndicate to furnish a definite amount of gold is not more important than the implied one expressed in the following clause "as far as lies in its power to exert all financial influences and make all legitimate efforts to protect the Treasury of the United States against withdrawals of gold pending the complete performance of the contract." The New York Evening Post, which is very close to the administration and which is a recognized financial authority, has called attention to the fact that Mr. Sherman when Secretary of the Treasury and about specie payments, employed the Rothschilds to do exactly the same thing. The Post cites the following letter from Mr. August Belmont to Secretary Sherman which it says is expressive of the spirit of the entire contract and of the motive which animates the managers of the syndicate.

"NEW YORK, April 10, 1878.—Hon. John Sherman—My Dear Sir, I take, so to say, the liberty of adding a few lines to my letter of to-day, in order to assure you that no question of rivalry, no wish of grasping the government business, and no pecuniary personal consideration of any kind prompts the opinion which I venture, at your invitation, to submit to your earnest attention.

"The syndicate to whom you have intrusted this negotiation, so essential to the success of resumption, are fully alive to the importance of this trust. Aside from the natural desire to secure the small legitimate banking commission on the transaction, their main object is and will be, as it has been in the past, to further as far as will be in their power the resumption of specie payments on the day fixed by law without unnecessary contraction and disturbance of the money market. To assist them in their efforts, they only ask at your hands that confidence and cooperation to which they think their management of the funding business for the last five years entitles them. Yours most truly, AUGUST BELMONT."

"Mark, do you know that it is nearly eight o'clock and that I promised to be at Armstrong's at eight-thirty? We must really go in now."

The man got up rather unwillingly; he was uneasy somehow about Ruth; she seemed to have raised a barrier between them, something that made him feel that she was less his than he had chosen to consider her.

Later that day it occurred to him that he had not thought of the Irish girl for several hours. He did not think of her until the moon rose and he went out on the headland, and sat alone with his pipe, and he longed to make her aware of the fact.

"Ruth, do you feel inclined to come for stroll?" The girl was sitting in a large basket chair in the garden; on her hand she held a magazine, but she was not reading it. She was looking out over the sea, thinking, thinking of something which called up a little smile to her lips.

She looked so sweet and fresh, and cool, her soft white gown showing her pretty, sunburnt cheeks and the glorious color of her hair. Mark approached her with his request almost efficiently. He was quite unhappy in those days, for as is usual in this life, he had not appreciated the good things life held for him until he felt he was likely to lose them.

To-day, however, Ruth willingly consented to accompany him. "Let us go on in the heather," she said, "and you must talk to me, for I am feeling fearfully lazy."

So they strolled along the narrow lane in springy beds of purple and white heather stretched away for miles, and the low hedges were draped with festoons of honeysuckle and "old man's beard." She claimed as she leaned back against a soft cushion of sweet-scented thyme, it was superstitious should say it was too good to be true.

"I think it is," said Mark rather mournfully. "We seldom have a walk or anything else together now, Ruth."

"No." She was not prepared for his suddenness, and determined to make the most of it. "Ruth, dear, you have changed lately; we are not such good friends as we used to be. Why is it? Tell me."

He looked up at her, and from his lowly position could see every change in her face.

"Don't be silly," she said, studiously averting her eyes. She stopped and gathered handfuls of heather which she promptly began to destroy and scatter in little showers over a mound. "Ruth, you must know. It is only fair that you should tell me why." Ruth, however, made no attempt to reply. "Won't you tell me?" he said wistfully. "You are making me very miserable, dear." His voice was quite sad and pleading. It touched the girl in spite of herself.

"I am? Oh, Mark!" The tears almost came into her eyes, but she smiled instead. "How can I make you unhappy?"

"Because I love you, Ruth, and cannot bear this something that has risen between us; it drives me mad, Ruth, my dear little girl. Don't you know how I love you and that I want you to be something very, very much nearer than a friend?"

The smile died away from her face; she grew very pale and her fingers trembled a little as she played with the heather, but she spoke calmly, almost coldly. "I did not know it was me you loved," she said.

"I have never loved any one else, not with real love such as I have for you. I may have admired others, yes, and perhaps thought myself in love with them for a time; but that is all."

WASHINGTON, April 3.—The income
tax returns are coming in far beyond the
expectations of the officials. As many as
10,000 returns have already been re-
ceived and are now being verified and
being recorded.

It is estimated that the returns made
to the collectors prior to March 10 repre-
sent at least $1,500,000 in income tax,
and that the actual amount returned by
April 1, will aggregate $15,000,000.

It is expected that at least $20,000,000
in income tax will have been collected
by June 1, the close of the fiscal year.
The officials do not express any doubts
that the Supreme Court will sustain all of
the important features of the law, if not
of the entire act as it stands, and are push-
ing the work as rapidly as is consistent
with accuracy.

ing Monday, May eth, indicate but

the continued cool, rainy weather.

parently not generally excessive,
but the spring has been so wet that
a small amount of rain makes the
ground too wet 10 plow.: But few
correspondents report the week a
good one for work, while all report
slow growth of crops. TIE tempe
nature was decidedly below normal
Light frost occurred over a large

did very slight damage. Showers

days of the week. Entire fields of
cotton are being plowed up on some
farms and corn or cotton planted
again. Corn is slow to recover from
the effects of recent frost: Melon
vines seem to be the special prey of
insects and they are being ruined in
many places. The cool weather is
very favorable for the work of cut
worms and potato bugs. Trans
planting of tobacco went on fairly

For a forcible lesson in economics as well as an insight into Oriental life and customs, the student of these subjects should not fail to visit a Japanese hotel in Honolulu. They abound chiefly in what is now popularly termed 'Japan Sea,' being the district fronting Kaumakapili church, though very choice hotels may be found on Nuuanu, on King and on other cross streets. These hotels are usually light and airy, and are not without social attractions. Music will be heard in most of them, games of various kinds are provided and not infrequently sake is to be had by guests. In the evenings crowds assemble in them, and sometimes the hotels become noisy.

Japanese hotels, as a rule, have only four or five sleeping apartments. There is in all of them one or two wee bedrooms, just large enough for a cot and wash stand, set apart for special guests who are willing to pay a larger rental. They cost from fifteen to twenty-five cents per day, or from $5 to $8 per month. The main sleeping rooms, however, showing the odd feature of the business, are large halls about 15 feet long by 8 wide. There are two and sometimes three in each. Upon the floor of these rooms, platforms, covering every inch of space, 6 inches above the floor, are raised. On this matting is laid, and the bed is complete.

These beds accommodate any number of people. In dull times fifteen or twenty are huddled in together. But when business is good two to three dozen are packed into a single room. Japanese hotels are operated on the American plan, that is to say, so much per day, week or month. Board includes lodging and dining. to recovery. Every means was tried, but
to no avail. The girls found it impossible
not to just hop out from the blankets in
order to run in and tell their next door
neighbors that it was decided to trim the
new hat, with heliotrope, or that it was
true that Cousin Fred was actually engag-
ed, all of which seriously retarded recov-
ery. It looked for a time indeed as though
funerals might become epidemic as well as
measles.

Finally the psychology teacher hit upon
a scheme that seemed likely to work. It
consisted in the few well girls stationing
themselves in turn at the bed of each in-
valid and criticising her most unmerciful-
ly. The success of the plan was simply
phenomenal. After but few brief mo-
ments of such treatment the patient broke
out into profuse and violent perspira-
tion. Recovery soon followed; the doctors
were overwhelmed at this fresh proof of
the influence of mind over matter and the
psychology teacher was a proud and happy
pedagogue.—New York Sun.

NEW STYLE OF PLAYING WHICH MAKES IT

MUCH LIKE THE ORDINARY GAME

Two-handed whist is being played at some clubs, a new variation has been introduced which makes it resemble more than ever the regular four-handed game and has infused interest in it. As has been before explained in the Tribune the game is played by dealing to each of the two players half of the cards, one at a time as in the regular game. The cards are then placed on the table in piles of two, so that each player has thirteen piles. The top card of each pile is turned up at the beginning of the game. This leaves thirteen cards in each hand exposed. Play begins with the non-dealer who plays one of his exposed cards, and the trick is taken, he turns up the card that was beneath it. In this way all the cards are finally exposed and played.

As two cards make a trick, there are naturally twenty-six tricks in all, thirteen of which it takes to make a book after scoring, which every trick counts one point. Thus, while it is possible to make thirteen points in one deal, it is also possible to have no count whatever, and in actual play it frequently happens that neither player makes point in a particular deal.

The variation of the game is to arrange the cards before described when the non-dealer begins the play. As soon as he has made the play he turns up the card played. The other player then plays and likewise exposes the card uncovered, the first player exposing the face of the card underneath the one played, if there be one, and the second player has the last play. This, of course, makes only thirteen tricks, and the regular rules of whist govern in counting the points. Of course, that it is played by two persons makes it an interesting pastime. There is more of the game as, naturally, it is impossible to tell the location of the cards turned down until they are exposed. Good players soon discover the presence of the principal cards in the hands of their partners and it is always a chance for considerable headwork and often for well-considered and brilliant plays.

by lowering his own record of 10 seconds for
the 100 yards by doing the dash in 10.4
seconds at Chicago during the past week.


The Intercollegiate Association is no
doubt very glad to claim him as its own.
He held the Championships in the 100
and 220-yard dashes in the Central Association of the A. A. L. in 1894.


Speaking of the 100-yard dash, it is
proper to state that the distance was first
made in 10.5 on the C. A. C. track on
Analostan Island on October 11, 1880,
by J. Owen, Jr.


IN ARCHERY CIRCLES AND RANGES.


Archery, which several years ago was
quite the rage here, bids fair to regain its popularity and possibly to increase it
during this season.


Messrs. L. W. Maxson and D. F. MCGOWAN
have long worked hard in the interest of
the sport and succeeded in having the last
tournament, which was a national event,
held in this city. It was a success in every
way.


Among those who take active interest
in the sport are Miss E. C. Cooke, who
won the ladies' flight championship by
sending an arrow 15 1/2 yards; Miss Nicely, Miss N. J. Cushman, Dr. Anderson,
Mrs. W. Mcfarland and J. S. Banker.


In the last national event our local
archers were very much in evidence in all
the ranges and rounds, including the
double york, double American, ladies'
national and ladies' Columbia rounds.


The national tournament will be held at
DAYTON, Ohio, on August 21, 22, and 23,
next, and promises to be memorable in
point of fine records and number of entries
in each event. Dr. J. W. Anderson and D.
F. MCGOWAN, of this city, are members of
the national executive committee.


COLUMBIA ATHLETIC CLUB.


The opening club regatta of the Columbia Athletic Club on Wednesday was a
complete success and must have been very
gratifying to Lieut. Baker, who has worked
hard to conduct it.


The eight-oared event was an interesting one, but the seniors were too much
for the juniors. The defeat of the latter
will not affect the effort to get out a
good strong junior eight for the Peoples
Regatta at Philadelphia on July 4. The
weak places in the waist of the boat
will be strengthened at once.


Magoe is one of the coming oarsmen of the
river. He lacks length for a stroke
but he has form and grit. He was
in two of the winning crews in the regatta.


Many of the football players are rowing
this season, and they will be a power
in the boats. Among them are Wells,
Seton, Tallmadge, Shields, Carter and
Boyle.


Blunt and Mann are rowing in their
usual good strong form.


Moar promises to be one of the strong
scullers of the season.


It seemed like old times to Charlie
Baker in the shells. He was in two of the
winning crews on Wednesday.


The indications are that the junior eight
of this year will be equally as strong as
last year's. If a good junior eight cannot be prepared in time for Philadelphia
why not send up an intermediate eight?


Another club regatta will be given shortly
and will include races for outrigger,
pleasure boats and swimming races for
the club championship.


Prof. Crossley is devoting most of his
time to Columbia Field, which is now in
excellent condition. The board of governors has decided to continue the work
on the track and to keep it in fine condition at all times, having in view other
bicycle meets and possibly fall track and
field open meeting.

I proved this by all the available statistics and reasoned it out that if you take any county like Clay, for instance, and cut off the taxes on personal property and buildings and distribute the amount thus cut off over all the removed from the holders of land with personal property and buildings on would fall on land now held idle, and only part of it would fall back on the improved land, thus making the taxes lower than now and on vacant land higher than now. So in the cities, I thought some of the taxes taken off our homes would fall back on vacant lots, and only a part would fall back on the lots where the homes stand. Now, really, it seemed to me, it would be true. I went to the SCISSORS office and got the figures, and found that my reasoning was correct and therefore I thought I believed in the single tax.

But now comes Mr. Donnelly and tells us with a wave of his hand that we are all mistaken, that the single tax will make the farmers pay all the taxes and leave the rich land owners of the cities, mines, forests, absolutely free. He says it and reiterates it with emphasis, so, of course, it must be true.
